subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Geography simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What does GNI per capita measure?
options: The number of people in employment
The average income per person from all sources, including income earned abroad
The percentage of people living in cities
The total value of a country's exports
questions.explain: GNI (Gross National Income) per capita is the total income of a country, including earnings from abroad, divided by its population. It is a common economic indicator of development.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite measure combining which three elements?
options: Population, area and urbanisation
Birth rate, death rate and migration
Life expectancy, education and income (GNI per capita)
GDP, exports and imports
questions.explain: HDI combines life expectancy, years of schooling/education and GNI per capita into a single index between 0 and 1, giving a broader picture than income alone.

questions.q: A country has a low GNI per capita but a much higher HDI than expected. What is the most likely reason?
options: It has invested heavily in health and education despite low income
It has a very high birth rate
It exports only raw materials
It has a large tourism industry
questions.explain: Because HDI includes life expectancy and education as well as income, a country that invests in schools and healthcare can score higher on HDI than its income alone would suggest.

questions.q: The 'development gap' refers to...
options: The difference in wealth and quality of life between richer (MEDCs) and poorer (LEDCs) countries
A gap in a country's exam results
The time zone difference between countries
The distance between two settlements
questions.explain: The development gap describes the widening difference in standards of living and wealth between more economically developed and less economically developed countries.

questions.q: Which activity belongs to the PRIMARY sector?
options: Teaching in a school
Fishing for cod at sea
Assembling cars in a factory
Writing computer software
questions.explain: The primary sector extracts raw materials directly from the earth or sea, such as farming, fishing, forestry and mining.

questions.q: Which sector involves high-level research, information and communication technology, and consultancy?
options: Tertiary sector
Primary sector
Secondary sector
Quaternary sector
questions.explain: The quaternary sector covers knowledge-based services such as research and development and ICT, distinct from the tertiary (general services) sector.

questions.q: As a country develops economically, how does its employment structure typically change?
options: Primary employment falls while secondary and then tertiary employment rise
Everyone moves into the primary sector
Tertiary employment falls to zero
The share of workers in all sectors stays the same
questions.explain: As development proceeds, workers move out of primary (farming) into secondary (manufacturing) and increasingly into tertiary and quaternary services.

questions.q: What is a Transnational Corporation (TNC)?
options: A local family-owned shop
A charity working in one country
A company that operates in more than one country
A government department
questions.explain: A TNC (or multinational) has its headquarters in one country but production, offices or sales in several others, e.g. Coca-Cola, Toyota or Nike.

questions.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE for a poorer country when a TNC opens a factory there?
options: Profits are usually sent back to the home country
It creates jobs and can bring new skills and technology
Local resources may be exploited
Working conditions are always poor
questions.explain: TNCs create employment and can transfer skills, training and technology to the host country. The other options are recognised disadvantages of TNC investment.

questions.q: Globalisation is best described as...
options: The growing interconnection and interdependence of the world's economies and cultures
The movement of people within one country
A reduction in international trade
Countries becoming more isolated from each other
questions.explain: Globalisation is the increasing links between countries through trade, investment, technology and the movement of people, goods and ideas.

questions.q: Which factor has most contributed to the global GROWTH of tourism?
options: Cheaper air travel, more leisure time and greater disposable income
Falling incomes worldwide
Fewer public holidays
A decline in advertising
questions.explain: Rising incomes, more paid holidays, cheaper and faster air travel and better marketing have all driven the rapid growth of international tourism.

questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of mass tourism for a destination area?
options: It creates jobs in hotels and restaurants
It brings in foreign currency
Litter, pollution and damage to fragile ecosystems
It improves local infrastructure such as roads
questions.explain: Environmental damage, congestion, litter and pressure on fragile ecosystems are common negative impacts of tourism; the other options are benefits.

questions.q: What is a key feature of SUSTAINABLE (eco) tourism?
options: Maximising visitor numbers regardless of impact
Building as many large resorts as possible
Meeting tourists' needs while conserving the environment and benefiting local people
Removing all local involvement in tourism
questions.explain: Sustainable tourism aims to minimise environmental damage, respect local cultures and ensure local communities gain, so the resource is preserved for the future.

questions.q: Which of these is a RENEWABLE energy source?
options: Coal
Natural gas
Geothermal power
Oil
questions.explain: Geothermal is renewable, using heat from within the Earth. Coal, gas and oil are non-renewable fossil fuels that will eventually run out.

questions.q: Which statement about NUCLEAR power is correct?
options: It is a renewable energy source
It produces large amounts of carbon dioxide during generation
It generates a lot of electricity with low carbon emissions but produces radioactive waste
It uses no fuel at all
questions.explain: Nuclear power produces large amounts of low-carbon electricity, but concerns include the disposal of long-lived radioactive waste and the risk of accidents.

questions.q: A strategy to MANAGE energy demand sustainably would be to...
options: Improve energy efficiency and increase the use of renewables such as wind and solar
Ban all electricity use
Rely only on imported oil
Burn more coal to guarantee supply
questions.explain: Sustainable energy management combines conservation and efficiency with a shift towards renewable sources to reduce reliance on finite, polluting fossil fuels.

questions.q: Which is a negative impact of economic activity (e.g. mining or industry) on the environment?
options: Reforestation of large areas
Improved air quality
An increase in biodiversity
Water pollution, deforestation and soil degradation
questions.explain: Industrial and extractive activity can pollute water and air, clear forests and degrade soils, reducing biodiversity and harming ecosystems.

questions.q: Acid rain, produced by burning fossil fuels, damages the environment mainly by...
options: Increasing crop yields everywhere
Adding useful nutrients to soils
Cooling the atmosphere and reversing warming
Killing trees and acidifying lakes and rivers
questions.explain: Sulphur and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels form acid rain, which damages forests, acidifies water bodies and harms aquatic life.

questions.q: In an agricultural system, which of these is an INPUT?
options: Harvesting the crop
Ploughing the field
The wheat sold at market
Rainfall, seeds, labour and fertiliser
questions.explain: Inputs are what goes into a farm (physical inputs like climate and soil, and human inputs like labour, seeds and fertiliser). Ploughing/harvesting are processes; the crop sold is an output.

questions.q: Which best describes SUBSISTENCE farming?
options: Rearing animals purely for export
Farming mainly to feed the farmer's own family, with little surplus to sell
Growing crops only in greenhouses
Large-scale farming to sell crops for profit on world markets
questions.explain: Subsistence farming produces just enough food for the farmer and their family, in contrast to commercial farming, which produces crops or livestock to sell for profit.
